messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 61
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Asian
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Non-profit Worker
  trauma_type: Life-threatening motor vehicle collision
  pcl5: 42

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Tactile (Texture): A specific texture associated with the event, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident, Crash Discussions: Talk about accidents
  Threat: Threat in Sounds: I am on high alert when I hear unexpected or loud sounds, Startle to Movement: Unexpected movement nearby causes me to react as if I am in danger, Flashbacks: Suddenly feeling or acting as if the stressful experience were actually happening again
  Memory: Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Reliving Event: When I remember the frightening event I feel like it is happening right now., Visual Memories: My memories of the frightening event are mostly pictures or images.

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Rajesh Patel is a 61-year-old South Asian American man who has worked for years in the administrative side of a nonprofit, the kind of job that usually suited his steady temperament and preference for being useful behind the scenes. He came to treatment after a life-threatening motor vehicle collision that he still described less as something that happened in the past than as something that could take hold of him again without warning. Before the crash he had driven regularly for work, visiting partner sites and attending meetings across the city. The collision occurred while he was in his car on an ordinary workday, and what stayed with him most vividly was not a coherent story from beginning to end but a sequence of sharply preserved images: the sudden sight of another vehicle where it should not have been, the violent instant of impact, the ruined cars afterward. Even now, when he tried to describe it, he spoke in pictures. He could see twisted metal and shattered glass with an immediacy that made him pause mid-sentence and grip the arms of his chair.

What made the event feel especially close in the present was how easily ordinary moments turned into reminders. A particular texture associated with the crash could unsettle him immediately. He struggled to explain it abstractly, but when his hand brushed against a similar surface, his body reacted before he could think. It was the kind of sensory contact that made him feel abruptly transported back into the vehicle, as if the collision were not over. He also found himself caught off guard by the sight of cars that had been hit in accidents. Passing a damaged vehicle on the roadside, or even seeing one in a parking lot with a crumpled side panel, could stop him internally. He would feel his attention lock onto the image, his chest tighten, and for a few moments he was no longer fully in the present. Conversations about accidents were similarly hard to bear. If coworkers at the nonprofit mentioned a highway pileup or a fender-bender on the commute, Rajesh would go quiet, his face tightening as he tried to stay composed while the same terror rose in him.

In the months after the collision, he came to dread these moments because they did not feel like memories in the ordinary sense. Remembering the event brought back the same terror he had felt at the time. He said that when the memory came, it did not arrive as a distant recollection but as if the crash were happening right now. At times he experienced sudden flashbacks in which he felt or acted as though he were back in the collision. His wife noticed that he could freeze or jerk in place, staring ahead with a look she had not seen in him before. Rajesh himself found these episodes humiliating and frightening. He had come to believe that his mind could betray him at any moment, especially when something around him shifted suddenly or made a loud noise.

That sense of danger followed him into daily life. Unexpected or loud sounds put him on immediate alert. In the office, a dropped file box, a slammed door, or a chair scraping sharply across the floor could make him tense all over. If someone moved suddenly beside him in a hallway or leaned unexpectedly into his cubicle, he reacted as if he needed to protect himself. He knew other people did not understand why he startled so hard, and this only made him more guarded. At work he began positioning himself carefully in meetings, preferring seats where he could monitor the room and avoid being surprised by movement near him. He was embarrassed by how much attention he paid to nearby motion and abrupt sound, but what frightened him most was the feeling that his body was responding to immediate danger, not to a memory.

Over time he narrowed his world in small, practical ways. He avoided lingering when coworkers talked about traffic collisions and tried to look away from damaged cars when he encountered them. His wife saw him pull his hand back from certain materials at home with an expression she recognized as fear, though he found it difficult to explain why. These habits accumulated. At the nonprofit he became less available for activities that might expose him to upsetting reminders, and colleagues noticed that he seemed more withdrawn and less at ease than he once had. At home he was often preoccupied, wary of being startled, and ashamed that an ordinary workday accident still had this power over him.

He finally sought help after realizing that the terror remained unchanged whenever the memory was stirred. He was not coming in to analyze the crash as a past event; he wanted relief from the feeling that it was still able to happen again inside him. He said he was tired of living as though any loud sound, sudden movement, conversation about accidents, or glimpse of a wrecked car might pull him out of the present. What he feared most was that this would become the permanent shape of his life. What he hoped for, more quietly, was to be able to go to work, sit with other people, and move through the world without bracing for the collision to return.
